chapter.title: Tools: what the intern is allowed to touch

cards.body:
The model never clicks anything. It writes a note, *send an email to Priya about the invoice*, and a piece of ordinary software reads the note and does the sending.

**A tool is a named action the model may ask for.** The list of tools is the list of things our new intern is allowed to touch, and nothing else on the desk exists for them.

cards.prompt: Your agent gets one task: find out if the café on Elm Street opens on Sundays. It has exactly one tool: *search the web*. What can it do?

options.text: Search, read the results, and tell you the answer.
Add the opening hours to your calendar.

whyNot.b: That's an action it has no tool for: phoning needs a 'make a call' tool on the list, and there isn't one.
whyNot.c: That's a different tool: writing to a calendar is a separate action nobody put on the desk.

cards.reteach: The agent can only ask for actions on its list. Search is on the list, so it searches. Phoning and calendars are not, so however much the text says 'I'll call them', nothing happens.

cards.title: What a tool actually is
cards.body:
A *tool* is three things: a name like *search_web*, a one-line description the model reads, and a small piece of code that does the real work. The model sees only the name and the description, like a menu with no kitchen.

When the model wants one, it writes a request in a fixed shape: tool name, then the details. *search_web, phrase: Elm Street café Sunday hours.* That is text. Nothing has happened yet.

Then the code runs the search for real and hands the result back as more text. **The model asks; the code acts.** Talking needs no tool at all: writing a summary is just the model's own words.

cards.title: The stapler it never had
cards.body:
Mara builds an agent to tidy her downloads folder. She gives it 2 tools: *list files* and *move file*. On the first run it lists 212 files, then writes 212 move requests, one per file, and her code carries each one out.

Then it writes a request for a tool called *delete file*. Her code answers: no such tool. The agent shrugs, in text, and reports it tidied everything it could. Nothing was deleted, because nothing in the office could delete.

cards.prompt: You're building an agent to find and summarise 3 recent news stories about electric bikes. Which tool list is enough for the job?

options.text: Search the web, open a web page.
Search the web, send an email.
Open a web page, move file.

whyNot.b: That's a tool the task never needs: sending email adds risk and no help, and the summary needs no tool, it's just words.
whyNot.c: That's a tidying tool, not a reading one: with no search, the agent can't find the stories in the first place.

cards.reteach: Ask what actions the task truly needs: finding pages and reading them. The summary itself is the model talking, which needs no tool. Anything beyond that is rope you're handing over for nothing.

cards.title: The list is the safety lever
cards.body:
You'd think the big safety question is how clever the model is. It's the opposite. A brilliant model with no tools can't hurt anything. A plain model with a *send money* tool can empty an account by lunch. **Risk lives in the tool list, not in the brain.**

So builders sort tools into readers and writers. Readers (search, open a page, list files) look at the world and change nothing. Writers (send, delete, pay, post) change it, and often can't be undone.

The riskiest tool to hand over is a writer that reaches outside your own computer. For the news task, that tool isn't on the list at all. That's the point.

Dev gives his email-sorting agent one convenient tool: *run any command*. It can read mail with that. It can also delete mail, and it does, 40 messages, while 'tidying'. How to spot it: if a tool's description contains the word *any* or *everything*, it isn't a tool. It's the keys to the building.

cards.prompt: Which sentence is true about how an agent acts?

options.text: The model performs each action itself, like a person at a keyboard.
The model writes a request naming a tool, and separate code performs the action.
The model can use any tool it learned about in training, listed or not.

whyNot.a: That's the picture from films, not the loop: the model only ever produces text, never a click.
whyNot.c: That's knowing about a tool, not having one: the intern may know what a phone is, but there's no phone on the desk.

cards.reteach: Picture the intern at a desk with a short menu. They write 'search this' or 'move that' on a slip, and someone else carries it out. Off the menu, the slip goes nowhere.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
An agent acts through tools: named actions the model asks for in text, which ordinary code then carries out. **Whatever is on that list is everything the agent can touch**, so the list is where the risk lives, not the cleverness.

Tomorrow: why an agent that worked for 10 steps starts repeating itself at 40.
Open ChatGPT or Claude and ask: 'What tools do you have right now, and what can't you do?' Sort the answer into tools (search, run code) and plain talking.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now list the tools an agent needs for a task and point to the one that is riskiest to hand over.
